# Analytic Techniques

> Copy of [Analytic Techniques](https://github.com/SOsintOps/intelligence-field-notes/blob/main/docs/analytic-techniques.md) from [Intelligence Field Notes](https://github.com/SOsintOps/intelligence-field-notes) 0.1.1. The original is the reference; this copy is here for offline use.

The mind is a poor instrument for judging incomplete and ambiguous information, and open sources are nothing but incomplete and ambiguous information. This page lists the cognitive traps that matter most in OSINT and the structured techniques that counter them. Its backbone is Richards Heuer's [*Psychology of Intelligence Analysis*](https://www.cia.gov/resources/csi/books-monographs/psychology-of-intelligence-analysis-2/): the biases cannot be switched off by knowing about them, only worked around by method.

## Cognitive Biases That Matter in OSINT
| Bias | What it does | OSINT example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Confirmation bias** | Seeking and over-weighting what supports the view already held | Reading only the channels that fit the narrative you started with |
| **Anchoring** | Over-relying on the first piece of information | Trusting the first username match without verifying identity |
| **Availability** | Over-weighting what is vivid, recent or easy to find | Studying the loudest accounts and missing the quiet, significant ones |
| **Mirror imaging** | Projecting your own logic onto the subject | Assuming a threat actor behaves "rationally" by your norms |
| **Attribution error** | Explaining behaviour by character rather than circumstance, or assigning authorship on style alone | Calling a hacktivist channel state-sponsored because of its tone |
| **Vividness and single-case reasoning** | A striking example outweighs dull statistics | One dramatic post taken as representative of a movement |
| **Premature closure** | Stopping the search once a plausible answer appears | Ending the investigation at the first company that "fits" |
| **Absence of evidence** | Ignoring what should be there and is not | Not asking why a supposedly active person has no trace on the platform where their peers are |
| **Automation bias** | Trusting a tool's or a model's output because a machine produced it | Reporting a face-match score or an AI summary as a finding |

## Habits That Reduce Bias
- Write the question and your initial hypothesis down at the start, so that you can see later how far you have moved.
- Make assumptions explicit, in writing, before they harden into facts.
- Look for evidence that would *disprove* your favourite hypothesis, not for more that supports it.
- Diversify sources: platforms, languages, types (official records, media, social, technical).
- Have someone else read the conclusions before they leave your desk.
- Treat any tool output (matching, scoring, translation, AI summary) as a lead to verify, never as a finding.

## Structured Analytic Techniques
Structured techniques externalise thinking: they put the reasoning on paper where it can be checked, criticised and repeated. The three families most useful to a single OSINT analyst are diagnostic, contrarian and imaginative.

### Key Assumptions Check (diagnostic)
List the assumptions the analysis rests on, including the ones that seem too obvious to state. For each, ask: why do I believe it? Under what conditions would it be false? Has it been true in the past? What would I see if it stopped being true? Any assumption you cannot support becomes a gap to collect against or a caveat in the report.

### Analysis of Competing Hypotheses (diagnostic)
Heuer's ACH replaces "which explanation do I like?" with "which explanations does the evidence rule out?". The eight steps:
1.  Identify the possible hypotheses, with more than one mind if possible. Include the uncomfortable ones and deception.
2.  List the significant evidence and arguments for and against each, including assumptions and the absence of expected evidence.
3.  Build a matrix: hypotheses across the top, evidence down the side. Mark each cell as consistent, inconsistent or not applicable. Look for **diagnostic** evidence: an item consistent with every hypothesis tells you nothing.
4.  Refine the matrix: reconsider the hypotheses, drop evidence with no diagnostic value.
5.  Draw tentative conclusions by trying to *reject* hypotheses. The one with the least evidence against it survives, not the one with most in favour.
6.  Test how sensitive the conclusion is to a few critical items of evidence. What if one is wrong, or planted?
7.  Report the conclusions, including the relative likelihood of all the hypotheses, not only the winner.
8.  Identify the indicators that would show events taking a different course.

### Indicators and Signposts (diagnostic)
For each hypothesis or scenario, list the observable events that would show it is happening. A list of indicators turns a static judgement into something that can be monitored, and tells collection what to look for next.

### Devil's Advocacy and Team A / Team B (contrarian)
Assign someone, or yourself in a separate session, to build the strongest case against the prevailing view. In Team A / Team B, two analysts or groups develop competing explanations in full and present them side by side. Useful precisely when everyone agrees: "when everyone agrees on an issue, something probably is wrong" (UNODC).

### High-Impact / Low-Probability and "What If?" (contrarian)
Assume an unlikely but damaging event has happened and work backwards: what would have had to occur, and would we have seen it? This exposes the indicators of the surprise you are not expecting.

### Premortem (imaginative)
Before finalising, imagine that the report turned out to be badly wrong six months from now. Write down why. The reasons are the weaknesses to fix or to state.

### Link, Timeline and Network Analysis
Visual techniques that organise entities and events: who is connected to whom, in what order things happened, where the network's centres and bridges are. They are tools to think with, not products; see the [UNODC manual](https://www.unodc.org/documents/organized-crime/Law-Enforcement/Criminal_Intelligence_for_Analysts.pdf), chapters 6 to 9, for the conventions.

## Deception and Manipulation
Open sources are written by people who know they are being read. Expect sock-puppet accounts, coordinated amplification, bought followers, recycled images, false-flag indicators and planted documents. Be most suspicious when a match is *too clean*: one high-profile indicator pointing at a well-known actor while everything else is ambiguous. Record the deception hypothesis in your ACH matrix and say in the report what you considered and why you accepted or rejected it.

## Further Reading
- **"Psychology of Intelligence Analysis"** by Richards J. Heuer Jr. (CIA Center for the Study of Intelligence, 1999) - Mental models, cognitive biases and the original description of ACH (chapter 8). [CIA page](https://www.cia.gov/resources/csi/books-monographs/psychology-of-intelligence-analysis-2/) · [PDF](https://www.cia.gov/resources/csi/static/Pyschology-of-Intelligence-Analysis.pdf)
- **"Structured Analytic Techniques for Intelligence Analysis"** (3rd edition, CQ Press / SAGE) by Randolph H. Pherson and Richards J. Heuer Jr. - Sixty-six techniques, organised by family, with when and how to use each. [SAGE](https://www.sagepub.com/en-us/cab/structured-analytic-techniques-for-intelligence-analysis/book255432)
- **"A Tradecraft Primer: Structured Analytic Techniques for Improving Intelligence Analysis"** (CIA, 2009) - A short, free introduction to the diagnostic, contrarian and imaginative techniques. [CIA page](https://www.cia.gov/resources/csi/books-monographs/a-tradecraft-primer/) · [PDF](https://www.cia.gov/resources/csi/static/955180a45afe3f5013772c313b16face/Tradecraft-Primer-apr09.pdf)
- **"Criminal Intelligence: Manual for Analysts"** (UNODC, 2011) - Inference development, link, event, flow and telephone analysis. [PDF](https://www.unodc.org/documents/organized-crime/Law-Enforcement/Criminal_Intelligence_for_Analysts.pdf)
